title: Document that docs/log.md does not preserve authored prose, and warn at sync time
description:
docs/log.md's CONTENT contract is undocumented, and a careful consumer built a test against the wrong expectation because of it.

parseEntries (src/core/log.ts) is total by construction: any line that is neither a folder heading nor an entry -- prose, a stray hand edit, the `# Change log` title, a blank -- is SKIPPED. A regenerated log is therefore a function of git history plus the entries still legible in the old file, and nothing else. Hand-authored prose placed in docs/log.md does not survive `lore sync`. That is deliberate, and the reasoning is good (the alternative, failing the sync, would leave a repo unable to run lore sync at all because of a file lore itself generated) -- but it is stated ONLY in a source doc comment.

docs/reference/cli-contract.md:33-38 is where a consumer looks, and it says log.md is "generated output refreshed from git history by lore sync", that it renders each documentation commit once, and that it is outside lore check's drift gate. It says NOTHING about what happens to content already in the file. A reader can reasonably infer "refreshed from git history" means new entries are added; nothing tells them their prose is dropped.

EVIDENCE THIS GAP IS REAL AND COSTLY, 2026-09-13: a consumer's validation suite asserted that arbitrary authored prose in the generated log would survive a sync. It does not, so the test failed, and the failure was reported as 0.6.1 not fixing the LCLI-474 clobbering defect. That report consumed investigation across THREE repositories -- purpose-built fixtures here, an independent non-reproduction by opum-cli-e2e, a third by opum-agent -- plus a serious proposal to provision a Windows CI runner to chase a platform hypothesis that turned out to be irrelevant. The consumer found and corrected their own expectation. Nobody was wrong about the code; the disagreement was about what the generated log PROMISES. See LCLI-484 for the full trail.

The false alarm is the evidence for this task. A documented contract, or a warning at sync time, would have caught it in one step instead of a round trip through three repositories.

acceptanceCriteria.text: docs/reference/cli-contract.md's docs/log.md paragraph states explicitly that the file is regenerated from git history plus the entries still parseable in it, and that any other content -- hand-authored prose, stray edits, the title line, blanks -- is NOT preserved across a sync

The doc says this is deliberate and gives the reason (a total parse degrades to 'carry forward what is still legible' rather than failing the sync and leaving a repo unable to run lore sync at all), so a reader does not file it as a defect

`lore sync` warns when docs/log.md contains unrecognised content that will be dropped, naming at least the count -- so a consumer learns at sync time rather than after a round trip through three repositories

`lore sync` reports a log summary: entries added, carried forward, and dropped. This is the part that would have made the LCLI-484 false alarm self-diagnosing, because the consumer would have seen the drop count move
A test covers the drop-and-warn path, so the documented contract and the implemented one cannot silently diverge later
